value.overview: The Common Gallinule is a duck-sized rail of marshes, ponds, lakes, and other wetlands. It swims well, walks across floating vegetation, and is recognized by its dark body, bright red-and-yellow bill and forehead shield, and white stripe along the flanks. Formerly called the Common Moorhen, it occurs across much of the Americas. In Costa Rica, it is a native wetland bird recorded in suitable freshwater habitats.
value.classification: The Common Gallinule belongs to the rail family, Rallidae, in the order Gruiformes. Its scientific name is Gallinula galeata; it was formerly treated as part of the more broadly defined Common Moorhen, Gallinula chloropus.
value.identification: Adults are mostly dark slate-gray to black, with a conspicuous red frontal shield and red bill tipped with yellow. A white stripe runs along the side, and white undertail feathers show when the tail is raised. The legs are greenish, and the long toes lack lobes or webbing. Juveniles are duller brown, with less distinct facial markings. It often bobs its head while swimming and walks with a crouched posture across mud or floating plants.
value.rangeHabitat: The Common Gallinule has a broad American range extending from Canada through the United States, Central America, and the Caribbean to much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is included on the national bird list and occurs in suitable wetland habitat, including marshes, ponds, lakes, flooded fields, rice areas, and quiet edges of canals or lagoons. It favors sites with a mixture of open water and dense emergent, floating, or submerged vegetation, generally in lowland and foothill areas.
value.migrationStatus: Movement varies geographically. Many populations are resident, while northern birds migrate south in winter. In Costa Rica, the species is recorded as a resident with possible migratory occurrence; it may be present year-round in suitable wetlands, with additional individuals potentially moving through the country.
value.breeding: Common Gallinules usually breed in freshwater or brackish marshes, ponds, and lakes containing dense emergent vegetation. Pairs build broad, bowl-shaped nests from grasses and sedges, usually on floating plant mats or among vegetation near the water’s edge; additional platforms may be built for resting or display. Clutches commonly contain 3–15 eggs, which are incubated for about 19–22 days. Chicks hatch covered in dark down and can leave the nest soon after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is varied and includes aquatic plants, grasses, sedges, seeds, grains, pondweed, duckweed, snails, insects, and other small aquatic invertebrates. The bird picks food from the water surface, mud, or vegetation and may dive or dabble in shallow water. It also flips leaves and plant material with its feet to expose hidden prey. In Costa Rica, it can forage in both natural wetlands and human-made ponds or flooded agricultural areas.
value.behavior: Common Gallinules are usually secretive, staying close to dense marsh vegetation while giving distinctive clucks, squawks, and whinnying calls. They swim with buoyant movements, walk on floating plants using their long toes, and may run across open mud or vegetation. Adults are territorial during breeding, whereas nonbreeding birds can gather in loose groups and associate with coots and ducks. Flight is generally labored, and birds often choose to escape by swimming or running into cover.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established. Regional monitoring in North America has recorded declines, although the species remains widespread and locally common where suitable wetlands persist.
